First listed: 2025-10-13 | Evaluation cutoff: 2026-11-10

- [YouTube: Inside America’s Economic Divide: AI, Tariffs, & The Fed | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZwoAJEzH99U) - 2025-10-13
- [Substack: Inside America’s Economic Divide: AI, Tariffs, & The Fed | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 29](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/inside-americas-economic-divide-ai-a09) - 2025-10-13

Earliest listed publication among matched versions, not proof of an unedited contemporaneous archive. Claim timestamps refer to the reviewed version.

## Summary

Eisman expresses a modest turn toward concern about a bifurcated economy, consumer stress and AI returns. His headline subtraction of total AI capex from annual GDP growth is invalid growth accounting and should not support the ex-AI stagnation thesis. Liesman offers qualified tariff concerns, acknowledges near-term resilience exceeded his expectations, discusses Fed political context, and ends with historical reflections on Russia. The episode repeatedly separates conditional mechanisms from precisely timed forecasts.

Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.

<a id="youtube-ZwoAJEzH99U-c002"></a>
### 002. Subtracting over $400 billion of AI capex from roughly $530 billion implied GDP growth shows that the economy excluding AI is almost flat.

**Wrong** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 1:46-2:41](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZwoAJEzH99U&t=106s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

The stated arithmetic is not a valid decomposition of GDP growth; this is a material error in the evidence offered for the core macro thesis.

Conditional reasoning: Even if all capex were domestic and prices constant, the investment contribution to annual growth would depend on I(t)-I(t-1), not I(t). If AI capex were $400b in both years, its direct growth contribution would be zero although the proposed subtraction removes $400b. Imports, overseas spending and inflation further prevent the claimed residual from measuring ex-AI real growth.

Assessment test: Inspect the relevant original financial, operational or economic data and compare the claimed mechanism with competing explanations.

Further verification: Recheck the original data and subsequent realized outcomes.

- [The expenditures approach to measuring GDP](https://www.bea.gov/index.php/news/blog/2025-06-03/expenditures-approach-measuring-gdp) (2025-06-03): GDP measures domestic production; expenditure components contain imports that must be subtracted. Global company capex therefore is not automatically US GDP contribution.

## Framework and tools

- Separate markets, corporate margins and domestic output.
- Use changes in domestic real investment when decomposing real GDP growth.
- Test consumer stress across multiple credit and spending categories.
- Evaluate policy forecasts under the policy actually specified.
- Trace who captures technological returns and who finances the buildout.
- Distinguish asset-price, employment and income-distribution channels.

Tools and charts discussed, not a complete visual inspection:

- GDP versus total AI capex arithmetic
- CarMax and auto-credit warning indicators
- Cruise versus hotel relative pricing
- Statutory versus collected tariff rates
- Fed communications and political constraints
- Financial-crisis leverage/asset/interconnection mechanism

## Source cautions

Steve Eisman interviews CNBC economics reporter Steve Liesman. Distinct host and guest claims are maintained; assent to a question does not transfer every guest forecast to Eisman.
- Opening montage repeats the body.
- All 1471 caption lines were read.
- Steve Liesman is repeatedly rendered Leeman or Leaf in captions.
- Market and GDP concern does not amount to an unconditional recession forecast.
- The $500 to $1500-$2000 hotel-price example is explicitly made up.
- Russia anecdotes and confidential market conversations are not independent empirical evidence.
